newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian premier dismisses talk that Yeltsin quit.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier dismisses talk that Yeltsin quit.

text.p: The Kremlin rallied round President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday and dismissed suggestions that he should quit, but brief television footage showed an almost motionless president who clearly found it hard to speak.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, quoted by Interfax news agency after a 40-minute meeting with Yeltsin, said he did not accept calls by communist rivals that Yeltsin should resign if he was unable to carry out his duties.
"This is out of the question now," Interfax quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.
Russian television stations released film of the president's meeting with Chernomyrdin, but the clip was heavily edited and it was not clear exactly what the two men had been discussing.

One sentence ended with the words "...council of doctors, operation...", but it was not clear if this was just an edited part of a fuller tape. Yeltsin sat almost motionless in one sequence, breaking into a broad smile in a second one.
But Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the president was in full control of Russia, working on documents for up to 2-1/2 hours a day.
Yeltsin, 65, has been in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital for the last 10 days while doctors get him ready for an operation to improve the flow of blood to his heart.
Yastrzhembsky said a council of doctors, including U.S. specialist Michael DeBakey, would meet the president on Wednesday to decide when to operate and exactly what to do.

DeBakey, 88, conducted the world's first successful heart bypass operation. He is in Moscow this week to attend a medical conference in the aptly named President Hotel, once the exclusive preserve of guests of top Kremlin officials.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year and he spent much of the second half of the year in hospital or in a sanatorium.
Top Kremlin doctor Renat Akchurin said at the weekend that Yeltsin might have had a third attack during the summer, between the two rounds of Russia's presidential election.
Akchurin, who suggested at that time that the operation could be postponed or even cancelled, said on Tuesday there was no chance of abandoning the surgery.

Yeltsin has already handed over some powers to Chernomyrdin, and has said the prime minister will take over all his duties while he has the operation. This will include assuming control of the "red button" controlling Russia's nuclear missiles.
But the Kremlin has been at pains to stress that Yeltsin is still able to carry out his duties, despite his disappearance for long stretches and a longer than expected stay in hospital.
The communists, defeated by Yeltsin in the election, this week accused the president and his team of misleading the electorate by concealing information about his health.

Gennady Seleznyov, the communist chairman of the lower house of parliament, on Tuesday called for more openness on Yeltsin's health and said doctors should release full details when they discuss when or whether to operate on him.
The communists say Yeltsin's absence has created a power vacuum and that top politicians are jockeying for position to prepare to launch presidential bids if he steps down.
But Chernomyrdin dismissed reports that the leadership was split. "I do not recognise any factions, there are no factions and there will be no factions while we are here," he said.

But tight lips in the Kremlin -- press officers often answer questions with the stock phrase "We have no information on that" -- has focused attention on the medical conference, now a media circus where reporters and television crews almost outnumber doctors.
German heart surgeon Hans Borst said he thought the experts would be happy to advise Yeltsin.

"Logically the Russians should use the expertise presented by a group of at least 12 foreigners who are very well versed in this type of surgery," he said. "All of us are rather curious about what is going to be the next step."
Yeltsin's long stay in hospital and doubts about the operation have sent shudders through Russia's financial markets.
Russian shares fell an average of three percent on Monday and prices fell further on Tuesday morning, before recovering slightly in the afternoon.
